weeks.title: Hello, little one
weeks.head: Your baby sleeps most of the day and night: 14–17 hours in 24 hours is typical for the first 3 months.
notice: Sleep comes in short stretches, day and night.
Feeding signs: hands to mouth, turning towards the breast or bottle, smacking lips.
care: Feed only breast milk or formula; babies need no water or other drinks for about the first 6 months.
Every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, in their own space in your room, with nothing soft in it.
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.
play: Hold your baby close and talk softly.
When your baby makes sounds, smile, act excited and talk back: this teaches taking turns in a “conversation”.

weeks.title: Crying is talking
weeks.head: Fussing and crying add up to about 2 hours a day on average in the first 6 weeks. That is normal.
notice: Crying is how your baby tells you they are hungry, tired, too hot or need a cuddle.
Some days are much fussier than others.
care: Ask your doctor about vitamin D drops: all babies need 400 IU a day from soon after birth, including breastfed babies.
play: Try holding, gentle rocking or a walk; take a break if you need one (put baby down safely first).
Cuddle and hold your baby often. You can’t spoil a baby by holding or responding to them.

weeks.title: Talk, read, sing
weeks.head: Talking, reading and singing to your baby from day one helps them understand language later.
notice: Your baby listens to your voice and watches your face.
Feeding signs of being full: closing the mouth or turning the head away.
care: If your baby isn’t hungry, it’s fine to stop feeding.
play: Read anything out loud, even your own book.
Sing to your baby.
Watch your baby’s signals: sounds and eye contact mean “play with me”; turning away, yawning or fussing mean “I need a break”.

weeks.title: Tummy time begins
weeks.head: Short tummy-time spells while awake build neck and shoulder strength. Work up to 30 minutes a day, spread out.
notice: Short lifts of the head while on the tummy.
Arms and legs moving a lot.
care: Tummy time is for awake, watched play only; sleep is always on the back.
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.
play: Lay your baby tummy-down on your chest or a play mat for a minute or two, several times a day, while you watch.
During tummy time, put a toy at eye level in front of your baby to encourage lifting the head (always stay with them).

weeks.title: Looking at you
weeks.head: Faces are your baby’s favourite thing to look at.
notice: By 2 months, most babies (3 in 4) look at your face and calm down when spoken to or picked up.
Your baby may watch you as you move around.
care: Keep your baby in the same room as you for sleep for at least the first 6 months, in their own cot.
play: Get close, face to face, and make slow, big expressions.
Hold a rattle to one side of your baby’s head, shake it, and see if they look for the sound.

weeks.title: First real smiles
weeks.head: Many babies start smiling back at you around now.
notice: By 2 months, most babies (3 in 4) smile when you talk to or smile at them.
Your baby may seem happy to see you when you walk up.
care: Crying still runs at about 2 hours a day for many babies; it usually eases after 8–9 weeks.
play: Smile and talk, then pause: give your baby time to answer with a look or a sound.
Put your phone away during play: limiting your own screen time helps you notice and respond to your baby.

weeks.title: First sounds
weeks.head: Soft sounds other than crying start to appear.
notice: By 2 months, most babies (3 in 4) make sounds other than crying and react to loud sounds.
care: At night keep lights low and voices quiet; in the day open curtains and play. Babies slowly learn night is for sleep.
play: Copy your baby’s sounds back to them, like a little conversation.
When your baby is upset, practise staying calm: talk softly, hold, rock or sing.

weeks.title: Strong neck
weeks.head: Head control is building fast.
notice: By 2 months, most babies (3 in 4) hold their head up when on the tummy, move both arms and both legs, and open their hands briefly.
care: First vaccines are due at 2 months (Singapore: 6-in-1, which includes hepatitis B dose 2).
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.
play: Keep up tummy time, a little more each day.
Talk and play with your baby during feeding, dressing and bath time.

weeks.title: 2-month check-in
weeks.head: Time to look back at the 2-month milestones and bring questions to your baby’s check-up.
notice: By 2 months, most babies (3 in 4) look at a toy for several seconds and watch you as you move.
care: 2-month vaccines: 6-in-1 (DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB) dose 1.
watch: If your baby misses several milestones, loses a skill they had, or you are worried, talk to your doctor and ask about developmental screening.
play: Take care of yourself too: parenting is hard work, and it is easier to enjoy your baby when you feel okay.
Lay your baby on a blanket with safe toys to reach for and kick at.

weeks.title: Calmer days ahead
weeks.head: For most babies, fussing and crying start to drop after 8–9 weeks.
notice: Longer awake times with more looking around.
care: Colic (long bouts of crying) becomes much less common after 9 weeks.
play: Short walks outside: name what you see.
Give easy-to-hold toys, like a rattle or a cloth book with colourful pictures.

weeks.title: Cooing conversations
weeks.head: Coos like “oooo” and “aahh” are coming.
notice: By 4 months, most babies coo and make sounds back when you talk.
care: Set steady routines for sleeping and feeding.
play: Talk, wait, and answer each coo; this back-and-forth builds language.
Sing while you gently move your baby’s arms and legs up and down, a little baby “exercise”.

weeks.title: Following with the eyes
weeks.head: Your baby tracks things that move.
notice: Crying is now about 1 hour a day on average (10–12 weeks).
care: Babies need no screen time at this age; talking and reading are better.
play: Lay your baby on their back and move a bright toy slowly left to right and up and down.
Hold your baby securely under the arms with their feet on your lap and let them bounce.

weeks.title: Smiling to get your attention
weeks.head: Your baby starts to start the conversation.
notice: By 4 months, most babies smile on their own to get your attention and chuckle (not yet a full laugh).
care: Keep sleep safe at naps too: on the back, flat and firm.
play: Play simple face games; see what makes your baby chuckle.
Play peek-a-boo: cover your eyes, uncover and say “peek-a-boo!”, and watch for a smile.

weeks.title: Reaching out
weeks.head: Hands are getting busy.
notice: By 4 months, most babies hold a toy you put in their hand and swing their arm at toys.
care: Don’t keep your baby in swings, bouncers or strollers for too long: no more than 1 hour at a time.
play: Hang or hold a toy within reach so your baby can bat at it.
Notice how your baby reacts to different things to learn what they like and don’t like.

weeks.title: Hands to mouth
weeks.head: Exploring with the mouth is how babies learn.
notice: By 4 months, most babies bring their hands to their mouth and look at their hands with interest.
care: Putting things in the mouth is how babies learn.
play: Offer safe things to mouth: nothing sharp, hot or small enough to choke on.
Copy your baby’s sounds and see how long you can keep the back-and-forth going.

weeks.title: Push-ups
weeks.head: Tummy time is turning into mini push-ups.
notice: By 4 months, most babies push up onto their elbows or forearms on the tummy and hold their head steady when you hold them.
care: From 4 months, 12–16 hours of sleep in 24 hours (including naps) is typical.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.
play: Get down on the floor at eye level during tummy time.
Use your baby’s name often (“Are you ticklish?”) so they learn it.

weeks.title: 4-month check-in
weeks.head: A good week to review the 4-month milestones.
notice: By 4 months, most babies open their mouth when they see the breast or bottle if hungry, and turn their head towards your voice.
care: 4-month vaccines (Singapore): DTaP-IPV-Hib dose 2 and pneumococcal (PCV) dose 1.
watch: If your baby misses several milestones, loses a skill they had, or you are worried, talk to your doctor and ask about developmental screening.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day.
Back-and-forth play: when your baby smiles, smile back; when they make sounds, copy them.

weeks.title: Laughing together
weeks.head: Real laughs are on the way.
notice: By 6 months, most babies know familiar people and laugh.
care: Breast milk or formula is still all your baby needs to eat or drink.
play: Find the games that make your baby laugh and repeat them.
“Read” every day by talking about colourful pictures, and answer your baby’s babble: “Yes, that’s the doggy!”

weeks.title: Teething may start
weeks.head: Most babies start teething around 6 months, but some start before 4 months and some after 12 months.
notice: Possible signs: sore red gums, more dribbling, chewing on things, a flushed cheek, fussier sleep.
care: Note teething signs in Goldfox so you can spot a pattern.
Teething can raise the temperature slightly, but not to 38 °C. There is no evidence teething causes diarrhoea.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day; more is better.
When your baby looks at something, point to it and talk about it.

weeks.title: Raspberries and squeals
weeks.head: Your baby plays with sounds.
notice: By 6 months, most babies take turns making sounds with you, blow raspberries and squeal.
care: Reading together every day supports language and bonding.
play: Blow raspberries back and take turns. Share a picture book and name what you see.
Sing to your baby and play music.

weeks.title: Grab and explore
weeks.head: Reaching is getting accurate.
notice: By 6 months, most babies reach to grab a toy they want and put things in their mouth to explore.
care: Check toys aren’t small enough to choke on.
play: Put toys just out of reach, on the tummy or back, to encourage rolling and reaching.
Hold your baby sitting up and give them toys to look at while they learn to balance.

weeks.title: Rolling over
weeks.head: Rolling opens up a new way to move.
notice: By 6 months, most babies roll from tummy to back.
care: The healthy age range for sitting without support starts around 3.8 months and runs to 9.2 months.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.
play: Give lots of floor play several times a day.
Hold your baby securely under the arms to stand, look around together and name what you see.

weeks.title: Mirror, mirror
weeks.head: Your baby is becoming interested in faces, including their own.
notice: By 6 months, most babies like to look at themselves in a mirror.
care: Some babies start standing with help from about 4.8 months; the normal range runs to 11.4 months.
play: Sit together in front of a mirror and name body parts.
Try different sounds: whisper, clap or make funny noises, and see which ones your baby likes.

weeks.title: Getting ready for food
weeks.head: Solids usually start around 6 months, not before.
notice: By 6 months, most babies push up with straight arms on the tummy and lean on their hands when sitting.
care: Talk to your doctor about when to start solids and which foods are choking risks. If your baby was premature, ask for specific advice.
play: Let your baby sit with you at family meals to watch how eating works.
When your baby drops a toy, pick it up and give it back. This game teaches cause and effect.

weeks.title: Hungry or full?
weeks.head: Learning your baby’s food signals makes mealtimes easier.
notice: Hungry: opening the mouth for a spoon, getting excited about food. Full: pushing food away, closing the mouth, turning away.
care: Follow your baby’s lead; how much they eat at first matters less than getting used to eating.
Introducing peanut-containing foods in infancy can help prevent peanut allergy. If your baby has eczema or a food allergy, ask your doctor first.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day; more is better.
Read your baby’s mood: if they’re happy, keep going; if they’re upset, take a break and comfort them.

weeks.title: Half a year!
weeks.head: Six months: first foods, new vaccines and lots of sounds.
notice: By 6 months, most babies close their lips to show they don’t want more food.
care: Start with small amounts alongside breast milk or formula; getting used to eating matters more than how much.
6-month vaccines (Singapore): 6-in-1 dose 3 and PCV dose 2. The flu vaccine is recommended every year from 6 months to under 5 years.
watch: If your baby misses several milestones, loses a skill they had, or you are worried, talk to your doctor and ask about developmental screening.
play: Share a book every day: reading together builds language and closeness.
Repeat your baby’s sounds and add a word: “bababa… book!”

weeks.title: First tastes
weeks.head: Variety from the start helps later eating.
notice: Most energy still comes from breast milk or formula.
care: Offer vegetables, including less sweet ones, not just carrot and sweet potato.
No added salt or sugar (including stock cubes and gravy). Cows’ milk can go in food, but not as a main drink until 1 year.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day; more is better.
Put toys a little out of reach and encourage crawling, scooting or rolling to get them. Celebrate when they do!

weeks.title: Naming the world
weeks.head: Your baby is starting to link words with things.
notice: By 9 months, most babies look when you call their name.
care: Allergens like egg, peanut, gluten and fish can be offered from around 6 months, one at a time, so you can spot any reaction.
play: On walks, point at cars, trees and animals and name them.
Teach waving “bye-bye” and simple baby signs so your baby can tell you what they want.

weeks.title: Safe finger foods
weeks.head: Food safety matters as textures get bigger.
notice: Gagging (watery eyes, tongue pushed forward, retching) is part of learning to eat.
care: Try soft finger foods your baby can pick up.
Avoid whole nuts and hard foods like raw carrot or apple. Cut small round foods like grapes into quarters.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day; more is better.
Play peek-a-boo with a cloth over your head and see if your baby pulls it off.

weeks.title: Peekaboo!
weeks.head: Games of hiding and finding are a hit.
notice: By 9 months, most babies smile or laugh when you play peekaboo.
care: Some babies stand alone from about 6.9 months; the normal range runs to 16.9 months.
play: Play peekaboo with your hands or a cloth.
Play “my turn, your turn” by passing a toy back and forth.

weeks.title: Mama-ma, ba-ba-ba
weeks.head: Babbling chains are coming.
notice: By 9 months, most babies make sounds like “mamamama” and “babababa”.
care: Keep reading every day; let your baby touch the pages.
play: Babble back and add the real word: “ba-ba… yes, ball!”
“Read” by pointing to pictures in books and naming them.

weeks.title: Bang, bang!
weeks.head: Making noise is science.
notice: By 9 months, most babies bang two things together and move things from one hand to the other.
care: Keep anything small enough to choke on out of reach.
play: Dump blocks out of a container and put them back in together.
Say a quick, cheerful goodbye instead of sneaking away, and announce it when you’re back.

weeks.title: A little shy
weeks.head: Stranger shyness is a normal sign of attachment.
notice: By 9 months, most babies are shy, clingy or fearful around strangers, and react when you leave.
care: Shyness with strangers at this age is expected, not a problem.
play: Let your baby warm up to new people from your lap.
Stay close while your baby explores so they know you’re near.

weeks.title: Where did it go?
weeks.head: Your baby knows things still exist when out of sight.
notice: By 9 months, most babies look for things dropped out of sight, like a spoon or toy.
care: Screen time is still not recommended under 1 year; reading and storytelling are encouraged instead.
play: Hide a toy under a cloth while your baby watches, then let them find it.
When your baby drops a toy, pick it up and give it back. This game teaches cause and effect.

weeks.title: On the move
weeks.head: Crawling has a wide healthy range: 5.2 to 13.5 months.
notice: By 9 months, most babies sit without support.
Some babies never crawl on hands and knees (about 4 in 100) and go straight to standing.
care: Give your baby safe places to explore: move sharp or breakable things out of reach.
play: Clear a safe floor space for exploring.
Try different sounds: whisper, clap or make funny noises, and see which ones your baby likes.

weeks.title: Feeding themselves
weeks.head: Messy eating is learning.
notice: By 9 months, most babies use their fingers to “rake” food towards themselves.
care: Let your baby practise finger foods and a cup with a little water. Sit together and expect spills.
Walking alone has a healthy range from 8.2 to 17.6 months, so there is no rush.
play: Share a book every day: reading together builds language and closeness.
Hold your baby securely under the arms to stand, look around together and name what you see.

weeks.title: Pick me up!
weeks.head: Your baby can ask with gestures.
notice: By 9 months, most babies lift their arms up to be picked up and show several facial expressions.
care: Keep offering new tastes and textures; it can take many tries before a food is liked.
play: Name feelings as you see them: “You look surprised!”
Play peek-a-boo: cover your eyes, uncover and say “peek-a-boo!”, and watch for a smile.

weeks.title: Sitting up solo
weeks.head: New positions, new views.
notice: By 9 months, most babies get to a sitting position by themselves.
care: Smooth, mashed or finely chopped foods all count as variety.
play: Ask for what you want to see: “time to sit” rather than “don’t stand”.
When your baby looks at something, point to it and talk about it.

weeks.title: 9-month check-in
weeks.head: Review the 9-month milestones; a general developmental screening is recommended at 9 months.
notice: By 9 months, most babies look when you call their name and bang two things together.
care: Ask about the 9-month developmental screening at your next visit.
watch: If your baby misses several milestones, loses a skill they had, or you are worried, talk to your doctor and ask about developmental screening.
play: Keep up daily floor play, reading and songs.
Back-and-forth play: when your baby smiles, smile back; when they make sounds, copy them.

weeks.title: Bye-bye!
weeks.head: Gestures are words before words.
notice: By 12 months, most babies wave “bye-bye”.
care: Keep offering foods your baby rejected before; tastes change.
play: Wave hello and bye-bye to people, pets and even the bathwater.
Talk or sing about what you’re doing: “This is the way we wash our hands.”

weeks.title: Understanding “no”
weeks.head: Your baby understands more than they can say.
notice: By 12 months, most babies understand “no” (they pause briefly or stop when you say it).
care: Babies should not be strapped in (pram, high chair, carrier) for more than 1 hour at a time.
play: Use short, clear words, and show what to do instead.
When your baby points, answer with words: “You want the cup? Here’s your cup.”

weeks.title: Pulling up
weeks.head: Furniture becomes a climbing frame.
notice: By 12 months, most babies pull up to stand.
Standing with help has a healthy range from 4.8 to 11.4 months.
care: Keep giving your baby safe places to explore.
play: Make sure what they pull up on is stable.
Point out interesting things you see, like a bus, a bird or a dog.

weeks.title: Cruising
weeks.head: First steps holding on.
notice: By 12 months, most babies walk while holding on to furniture.
Walking with help ranges from 5.9 to 13.7 months.
care: Being active several times a day is good for babies; more is better.
play: Place toys along the sofa to encourage cruising.
Give pots and pans or a small drum and let your baby make noise.

weeks.title: Pincer grasp
weeks.head: Tiny fingers, tiny bits.
notice: By 12 months, most babies pick things up between thumb and pointer finger, like small bits of food.
care: Offer soft small finger foods to practise.
Cut small round foods like grapes and cherry tomatoes into quarters.
play: Share a book every day: reading together builds language and closeness.
Share books with things to touch or flaps to lift.

weeks.title: Mama or dada
weeks.head: A special name for you is coming.
notice: By 12 months, most babies call a parent “mama”, “dada” or another special name.
care: Talk through everyday tasks; every word counts.
play: Build on what your baby says: if they say “ta”, say “Yes, a truck!”
Play together with blocks and other toys that get little hands working.

weeks.title: In and out
weeks.head: Putting things in containers is a big thinking step.
notice: By 12 months, most babies put something in a container, like a block in a cup.
care: Floor play several times a day is how babies practise new skills.
play: Play “in and out” with blocks and a box.
Show the behaviour you want and praise it with words and hugs, like stroking a pet gently.

weeks.title: Hide and seek
weeks.head: Your baby remembers where things went.
notice: By 12 months, most babies look for things they see you hide, like a toy under a blanket.
care: Keep reading together daily; let your baby choose the book.
play: Hide a toy under one of two cups and let your baby find it.
With a new caregiver, give your baby time to get to know them and bring a favourite toy or blanket.

weeks.title: Baby-proofing round two
weeks.head: A mobile baby needs a safer home.
notice: New reach: shelves, cupboards, bins.
care: Move sharp or breakable things out of reach; lock away medicines, chemicals and cleaning products. Save your local poison or emergency number in your phone.
play: Get down to baby height and look for hazards.
Teach waving “bye-bye” and simple baby signs so your baby can tell you what they want.

weeks.title: Cup practice
weeks.head: Drinking skills are developing.
notice: By 12 months, most babies drink from a cup without a lid while you hold it.
care: Offer water in an open cup with meals.
Drinks: water, breast milk or formula. No sugary drinks; juice isn’t needed.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day; more is better.
Play “my turn, your turn” by passing a toy back and forth.

weeks.title: Pat-a-cake
weeks.head: Games with rules and rhythm.
notice: By 12 months, most babies play games with you, like pat-a-cake.
care: Still no screen time recommended; shared reading, songs and play are best.
play: Sing action songs and pause before the clap so your baby can join in.
Say a quick, cheerful goodbye instead of sneaking away, and announce it when you’re back.

weeks.title: Sleep before one
weeks.head: 12–16 hours of sleep a day (including naps) is typical up to 12 months.
notice: Every baby’s sleep is different, and Asian babies on average sleep a little less in studies.
care: From 1 to 2 years, 11–14 hours a day is typical.
play: Keep the bedtime routine the same each night: bath, book, song.
Repeat your baby’s sounds and add a word: “bababa… book!”

weeks.title: Happy first birthday!
weeks.head: One year! Look back at how far your baby has come.
notice: By 12 months, most babies pull up to stand, wave bye-bye and understand “no”.
Many babies walk alone after their first birthday; the healthy range runs to 17.6 months.
care: 12-month vaccines (Singapore): MMR dose 1, chickenpox (varicella) dose 1 and the PCV booster. Cows’ milk can now be a main drink.
watch: If your baby misses several milestones, loses a skill they had, or you are worried, talk to your doctor and ask about developmental screening.
play: Celebrate with your baby’s favourite song and a photo for Moments.
Put toys a little out of reach and encourage crawling, scooting or rolling to get them. Celebrate when they do!
